Slides.Title: Creating a Prototype with Figma
Bullets: A step-by-step guide to building interactive prototypes from low to high fidelity using Figma.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: Welcome students to this module on prototyping with Figma. By the end of this session, you will be able to construct a low-to-high fidelity interactive prototype of your own interface project. We will walk through the entire process, from understanding what prototyping is, to publishing a polished, interactive design ready for user testing or presentation.

Slides.Title: What Is Prototyping?
Bullets: A prototype simulates user interaction before development begins.
Prototypes range from rough sketches to polished interfaces.
Fidelity describes the level of detail and realism.
Prototypes help validate design decisions early.
Figma supports the full low-to-high fidelity spectrum.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: Prototyping is a core practice in UX and interface design. Rather than building a fully coded product, designers create simulated versions of the interface to test ideas quickly. Fidelity refers to how closely the prototype resembles the final product — low-fidelity prototypes use simple shapes and placeholder text, while high-fidelity prototypes include real colors, typography, and interactions. Figma is an industry-standard tool that supports the entire prototyping workflow from concept to interactive mockup.

Slides.Title: Getting Started in Figma
Bullets: Create a free account at figma.com.
Figma runs in the browser — no install required.
Start a new design file from your dashboard.
Set up frames to define your screen sizes.
Use the toolbar to access shapes, text, and components.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: Students should begin by creating a Figma account if they do not already have one. Figma is browser-based, making it accessible on any computer. Once logged in, create a new design file and set up frames — these act as individual screens in your prototype. Choose a frame preset that matches your target device, such as a mobile or desktop screen. Familiarize yourself with the left panel (layers and assets), the canvas, and the right panel (design and prototype properties).

Slides.Title: Building a Low-Fidelity Prototype
Bullets: Use simple shapes and placeholder text for layout.
Focus on structure and user flow, not aesthetics.
Wireframes represent navigation and content hierarchy.
Grey boxes and lines indicate images and dividers.
Low-fi prototypes are fast to create and easy to change.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: A low-fidelity prototype, often called a wireframe, is your starting point. Use rectangles, lines, and placeholder text to map out where elements will appear on each screen. At this stage, do not worry about colors, fonts, or images — the goal is to define the layout and flow. This makes it easy to gather quick feedback and make changes without a large time investment. Encourage students to sketch on paper first, then translate those sketches into Figma frames.

Slides.Title: Connecting Screens with Interactions
Bullets: Switch to Prototype mode in the right panel.
Drag a connector from one element to another frame.
Set triggers: On Click, On Hover, After Delay, etc.
Choose transitions: Instant, Dissolve, Smart Animate.
Connected screens form a clickable user flow.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: To make your prototype interactive, switch from Design mode to Prototype mode using the tab in the top-right panel. Select an element — such as a button — and drag the blue connector arrow to the destination frame. You will then set the trigger (what the user does) and the action (what happens next). Common triggers include On Click and On Hover. Transitions like Smart Animate can create smooth, realistic animations between screens. Building these connections turns your static frames into a clickable prototype.

Slides.Title: Refining to Mid-Fidelity
Bullets: Add real typography and a basic color palette.
Replace placeholder boxes with actual UI components.
Use Figma's component library for consistency.
Apply auto layout to create responsive, flexible frames.
Mid-fidelity bridges wireframes and final design.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: Once your wireframe structure is validated, begin adding visual detail to move toward mid-fidelity. Introduce your chosen fonts and a limited color palette. Replace grey placeholder boxes with real UI elements like buttons, input fields, and navigation bars. Figma's component system lets you create reusable elements that update globally when edited. Auto Layout enables your designs to resize and adapt dynamically, mimicking real responsive behavior. At this stage, the prototype begins to look and feel closer to a finished product.

Slides.Title: Achieving High-Fidelity Design
Bullets: Apply final brand colors, imagery, and icons.
Use real content — actual text, photos, and data.
Add micro-interactions and advanced animations.
Ensure visual consistency across all screens.
High-fidelity prototypes closely resemble the final product.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: A high-fidelity prototype looks and behaves like the real application. At this stage, apply your full visual design: finalized brand colors, typography, real imagery, and icons. Replace all placeholder content with actual text and data. Use Figma's advanced prototyping features — such as component variants and overlays — to simulate micro-interactions like dropdown menus, modal dialogs, and error states. Review every screen for visual consistency in spacing, alignment, and style before presenting or testing.

Slides.Title: Previewing and Testing Your Prototype
Bullets: Click the Play button to launch Prototype Preview.
Navigate your prototype as a real user would.
Use Figma Mirror to preview on a mobile device.
Share a prototype link with collaborators or testers.
Gather feedback and iterate on your design.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: Figma's built-in Preview mode lets you interact with your prototype exactly as a user would. Click the Play button in the top-right corner to launch the preview. You can also use the Figma Mirror app to display your prototype live on a smartphone for realistic mobile testing. Share a prototype link with peers, instructors, or usability test participants without requiring them to have a Figma account. Use the feedback you collect to identify pain points and refine your design — iteration is a key part of the design process.

Slides.Title: Best Practices for Prototyping
Bullets: Start simple — add detail progressively.
Name frames and layers clearly for easy navigation.
Use components to avoid duplicating work.
Test with real users at each fidelity stage.
Document design decisions in comments or notes.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: Effective prototyping follows a progressive approach: start with the simplest version that answers your design question, then add detail as decisions are validated. Keep your Figma file organized by naming all frames, layers, and components descriptively — this is especially important when collaborating. Leverage the component system to save time and maintain consistency. Test your prototype with actual users at low, mid, and high fidelity stages to catch problems early. Use Figma's commenting feature to annotate decisions and communicate with team members or instructors.

Slides.Title: Summary: Your Figma Prototype Journey
Bullets: Prototypes validate ideas across all fidelity levels.
Figma supports the complete design workflow in one tool.
Interactions and transitions bring your screens to life.
Iteration based on feedback improves your final design.
You can now build a full interactive prototype in Figma.
Slides.SpeakerNotes: In this module, students progressed from understanding what a prototype is to constructing a complete low-to-high fidelity interactive prototype in Figma. You learned how to set up frames, build wireframes, connect screens with interactions, refine visual design, and share your prototype for feedback. The key takeaway is that prototyping is an iterative process — each stage of fidelity serves a purpose and informs the next. Apply these skills directly to your interface project, moving systematically from concept to a polished, interactive prototype ready for presentation or user testing.
